title: Why HubSpot Stock Rallied Today
detail:
Why HubSpot Stock Rallied Today
Danny Vena, CPA, The Motley Fool
Thu, October 22, 2026 at 12:23 PM MST 3 min read
HUBS
NVDA
CRM
BRZE
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Shares of HubSpot (NYSE:HUBS) charged sharply higher on Thursday, surging as much as 7%. As of 2:44 p.m. ET, the stock was still up 6.1%.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The catalyst that sent the cloud-based customer relationship management (CRM) specialist higher was chatter about recent mergers and acquisitions and what it could mean for the future.

Image source: Getty Images.

It only takes a spark

A wave of recent acquisitions in the software space has Wall Street analysts speculating about the future, and HubSpot came up in the conversation.

Earlier this week, Salesforce announced its intention to acquire Braze, a leading customer engagement platform, in a deal valued at $5.66 billion, representing a 58% premium over the prior day's closing price. This marked the third such major acquisition of a small- to mid-cap software company in recent weeks.

Just last week, cloud software and artificial intelligence (AI) company CCC Intelligent Solutions agreed to be taken private by a group of private investment firms including GTCR and Elliot Investment Management for $6.1 billion, marking a 44% premium. On the same day, cybersecurity provider Varonis Systems agreed to be acquired by privately held competitor Proofpoint for $6.3 billion, a 52% premium to the stock price prior to the rumored sale.

In the wake of this tidal wave of merger mania, Jefferies analyst Samad Samana has surveyed the landscape and believes there are more deals to come. He posits that the Braze buyout could be the "the spark that could lead to a strategic takeout" of rival Klaviyo. The analyst goes on to suggest that while he views an acquisition of HubSpot as unlikely, the company could be an attractive candidate for private equity.

Acquiring HubSpot would be a more costly affair, as the company has a market cap of more than $13 billion (as of this writing) -- and that doesn't include any premium shareholders would require to approve such a deal. Assuming the average premium of 51% for the above-cited deals, any acquisition of HubSpot would be in the neighborhood of $20 billion.

Like many software-as-a-service (SaaS) stocks, HubSpot has been punished in recent years as investors feared competition from AI, though the reality has proven to be more complicated. However, with the stock price near a five-year low, HubSpot could be an attractive acquisition for a company with deep pockets.

DocuSign recently expanded its more than 20 year Salesforce relationship by embedding its Intelligent Agreement Management platform into Salesforce, Agentforce, and Slack, and also launched DocuSign PDF Editor to connect desktop document preparation directly into its IAM and eSignature workflows.

Together, the deeper Salesforce integration and new PDF Editor suggest DocuSign is trying to pull more of the agreement lifecycle into its own ecosystem. This can matter for customer stickiness, workflow efficiency, and how much value large enterprises place on its IAM platform.

We will now see how DocuSign's broader IAM footprint inside Salesforce and new PDF Editor could influence the existing investment narrative.

Capture this agreement-automation momentum by scanning a curated set of SaaS and workflow platforms with resilient unit economics in the 21 high quality undiscovered gems.

DocuSign Investment Narrative Recap

For DocuSign, the core belief is that agreement management keeps shifting from simple e signatures to full lifecycle automation, where IAM, AI agents, and deep ecosystem hooks become everyday tools for large enterprises. The Salesforce, Agentforce, and Slack integrations point to that direction, but the key near term catalyst still sits in whether IAM mix gains start to show up clearly against today's high single digit revenue growth.

The biggest operational risk stays the same. If large deal activity and international expansion do not justify the investment in complex IAM deployments, and if cloud migration and hosting costs keep non GAAP gross margins around the low 80% range for longer, investors could keep treating DocuSign as a slower growth productivity vendor rather than a higher value workflow platform.

The Salesforce partnership update is the most relevant development right now. IAM embedded inside Salesforce, Agentforce, and Slack means sales, legal, and operations teams can move from draft to renewal inside the CRM and collaboration stack, with contract data feeding AI agents for term tracking, renewal alerts, and risk surfacing. That connects tightly to the thesis that IAM needs to justify a much larger share of ARR over time.

Execution is where this either reinforces or undercuts the current catalyst. If users actually run more of the agreement lifecycle inside Salesforce and Slackforce using DocuSign, that supports larger deal sizes and more durable workflows, which the existing narrative already flags as important. If adoption is slower or complexity causes friction, the risk around large enterprise focus and cautious guidance remains front and center.

The agreed US$5.9b all-cash takeover by Salesforce at US$47.50 per share concentrates attention on whether Braze's underlying cash flow profile can support that valuation level as fair for existing shareholders.

Is Braze a Bargain on Cash Flow?

The Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model here projects the cash Braze could return to shareholders based on its current and future free cash flows. Over the latest twelve months the business produced about $73.94m in free cash flow, and the model then extends this with a growing cash flow profile that reaches over $200m a year in the early 2030s.

Those rising projections help explain why the DCF output places Braze's estimated intrinsic value modestly above the current share price of $45.68. The latest analyst update for Braze lifts the Fair Value Estimate from US$36.25 to about US$40.54 per share, which now sits closer to the agreed US$47.50 cash offer from Salesforce. Recent research has shifted toward the deal terms and what this takeout price means for Braze holders, so the refreshed target levels are clustering around that reference point rather than an open ended standalone case. As you read on, you will see how this evolving narrative could shape what to watch next around the stock and the deal.

Stay updated as the Fair Value for Braze shifts by adding it to your watchlist or portfolio. Alternatively, explore our Community to discover new perspectives on Braze.

What Wall Street Has Been Saying
🐂 Bullish Takeaways

Several firms, including Stifel, Canaccord, Barclays and DA Davidson, had previously raised Braze price targets into the US$33 to US$40 range, pointing to customer wins, AI features and partner feedback as supportive for execution and longer term growth prospects.

DA Davidson now describes Salesforce's acquisition of Braze as a positive use of capital, citing Braze's valuation relative to its own trading history and the potential for Salesforce to use Braze to strengthen weaker areas of its platform.

Jefferies and DA Davidson see Braze adding meaningful capabilities and talent to Salesforce Marketing and Commerce Cloud, with Jefferies highlighting prior deal activity at Braze as evidence of an active product and M&A playbook.

🐻 Bearish Takeaways

Following the agreed US$47.50 per share cash offer from Salesforce, almost all covering firms such as Citi, UBS, Mizuho, Piper Sandler and Barclays have moved ratings to Neutral or Hold. This signals limited expected upside from current deal terms.

Evercore and Raymond James flag debate around the timing and price of the Salesforce deal, with some commentary that a higher competing bid looks unlikely and that the premium already reflects a fair outcome for existing Braze shareholders.

title: How Did Strategy Stock Leave Its Industry Behind?

How Did Strategy Stock Leave Its Industry Behind?

Over the five years to October 20, 2026, one stock outperformed 117 of the 125 other companies in its industry. That stock is Strategy (MSTR), the bitcoin treasury company formerly known as MicroStrategy, and its industry is Application Software. Before sizing a position on that record, an investor should understand where the gain originated. So was it the industry Strategy sits in, or Strategy itself?

How Far Strategy Is Ahead Of Its Industry

Shares of Strategy rose 88.2% over those five years, while the typical Application Software company fell 46.1%. The table below displays figures for the median company across the industry, sector and all-stock groups, alongside the S&P 500 index.

While a position in the typical software stock lost close to half its value, an investment in Strategy nearly doubled. The resulting performance gap places Strategy ahead of all but a handful of its industry peers.

Was It Strategy's Industry?

No, though the S&P 500 index provided a lift. The S&P 500, dominated by the largest companies, rose 70.0% over the same five years. Strategy stock still finished ahead of the index.

The company's own industry operated as a drag. Among the 12 industries within the Information Technology sector, Application Software ranked 11th based on the typical company's five-year return. The typical technology stock also fell. Strategy rose against the tide of its own group.

What Did Strategy's Business Do?

Sales at Strategy remained flat. Revenue growth averaged 0.02% a year over the past three years, compared with 11.1% for the typical software company. Between 2021 and 2026, revenue slipped 1.7%.

Profit per share moved the wrong way, from a loss of $4.33 a share in the twelve months to June 2021 to a loss of $97.21 in the twelve months to June 2026. The operating margin shifted from a 14.3% profit in the twelve months to June 2021 to an 8.1% loss in the twelve months to June 2026. Over those same years, the diluted share count rose 261.7%, leaving each share with a smaller slice of a business that loses money. Strategy reported an $8.22 billion loss in the quarter ended June 30, 2026, compared with a $10.02 billion profit a year earlier, as the bitcoin price declined, the WSJ reported. Over the past year, the company's net loss amounted to more than 60 times its revenue.

title: Salesforce (CRM) vs Oracle (ORCL): Which Is a Better Stock to Buy?
detail:
Salesforce (CRM) vs Oracle (ORCL): Which Is a Better Stock to Buy?
Suraj Santlani
Wed, October 21, 2026 at 11:08 AM MST 4 min read
CRM
ORCL
SPY
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Salesforce, Inc. (NYSE:CRM) closed at $242.45 on October 19. The stock returned 30.2% over the last 6 months, compared with an 11.6% return for the Insider Monkey Billionaire Index and 8.7% for the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust.

Oracle Corporation (NYSE:ORCL) closed at $129.59 the same day and has gone the other way, shedding more than a quarter of its value over those six months. Two of the largest businesses in enterprise software, pulled apart by half a year of trading. Salesforce sells the system companies run their customer relationships through. Oracle sells databases and rents out the computing capacity that artificial intelligence models are trained on.

READ ALSO: 10 Best Fundamental Stocks to Invest in According to Billionaires

Salesforce (CRM) vs Oracle (ORCL): Which Is a Better Stock to Buy?
What Salesforce Has:

The customer record lives in Salesforce, and so do the workflows the sales and service teams run on top of it. Replacing that means moving years of history and retraining the people who use it daily, which is why a slowing Salesforce is not a shrinking one. It converts about a fifth of revenue into operating profit and produced $14.4 billion of free cash flow in its last financial year.

What it lacks is growth. Revenue rose 10.80% in the most recent quarter, and the company is now buying what it cannot generate, agreeing on October 20 to pay $5.66 billion for the marketing software business Braze. The bigger risk sits in how it charges. Salesforce sells seats, so if software agents take on work that staff used to do, customers need fewer of them.

Both names appear in our 10 Most Promising Cloud Stocks According to Hedge Funds. To see the full ranking, click HERE.

What Oracle Has:

Oracle grew revenue 29.60% in the quarter just reported on a 35.63% operating margin, and underneath that sits the oldest annuity in software. Companies keep their most important records in Oracle databases, and the support that goes with them renews whether or not anything new is bought. That revenue pays for the build. What the market is being asked to price is the newer half, where Oracle rents capacity to companies training artificial intelligence models on contracts signed years in advance.

The build is the risk. Debt reaches 251.72% of equity, more than twice what Salesforce carries, and Oracle finished the past year with levered free cash flow of negative $45.85 billion despite generating a great deal from operations. Renting capacity also earns a thinner margin than licensing software, so faster revenue is not automatically the better business.

Meanwhile, ServiceNow (NYSE:NOW) stock is up 3% to $153.33, trailing Palantir stock while still beating the software fund. Salesforce (NYSE:CRM) stock is down 0.2% to $242.07, missing out on the rally that's lifting its software neighbors. That difference puts Palantir out in front of a rally that's leaving Salesforce behind for now.

On October 19, Knox Systems announced a partnership with Palantir to bring commercial software into the federal government's most tightly secured cloud environments. Under the arrangement, Palantir's federal accreditations serve as the route to deployment, and neither company disclosed financial terms. Because the announcement precedes this session, its link to Palantir stock's gain is an open question that the stock's trading alone can't settle.
